title: Skills at work: New evidence on returns to skills and training (OECD Employment Outlook 2026, Chapter 4)
key_claim: Analysis of PIAAC Cycle 2 (2022-2023, 31 countries) finds the association between years of education and wages fell by 2.2 p.p. between cycles. Participation in job-related formal education fell by more than 2 p.p. to 8% of adults, and non-formal job-related learning fell by 3 p.p. to 37%. Non-formal learning carries a wage premium of about 6.2%; training in teamwork, leadership and project management shows the largest premium, exceeding 8.5%; reading, writing, languages, computer and software and communication training sit at about 5.5% to 8.5%. Health and safety is the most common training type, over one-quarter of all training undertaken. Low-return topics account for about 40% of in-person training, and more than 40% of workers completing certificate-granting training did so in topics with relatively low wage associations. Six topics account for over 70% of employer-funded training, and more than 85% of employer-funded training happens in working hours. Very short courses do as well as long ones, and online or hybrid delivery performs at least as well as in-person.
frame_summary: The chapter is arguing that formal education and cognitive skills are losing their grip as the route from human capital to pay, so policy and employers should pivot toward making skills directly visible and toward the learning that demonstrably pays: short, flexible, non-formal training in teamwork, leadership and project management.

title: Executive summary (OECD Employment Outlook 2026: Geographic Disparities in Jobs and Incomes)
key_claim: The summary reports OECD employment rates at 72.1% on average in Q1 2026, historically high. On skills it states that PIAAC Cycle 2 evidence shows numeracy and formal education remain strong predictors of employment and wages, although their influence has weakened over the past decade. It also reports that one-third of workers in the OECD countries analysed are bound by non-compete clauses.
frame_summary: The executive summary is arguing that geography rather than individual skill is a first-order determinant of jobs and incomes, and that education and numeracy still predict outcomes strongly even though their influence has weakened, which is a materially more cautious reading than the chapter's own opening line.

title: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
date_evidence: eli:date_document: 2026-07-08 ; concluding formula 'Done at Strasbourg, 8 July 2026' ; OJ L series masthead 24.7.2026 ; eli:first_date_entry_in_force: 2026-07-27
key_claim: Article 1, point (5) replaces Article 4 of the AI Act. Providers and deployers must now take measures to support the development of AI literacy among staff, and the provision states expressly that the obligation does not require them to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual. Recital 8 records that stringent obligations to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy would not be suitable for all providers and deployers. The Regulation entered into force on 27 July 2026; Article 4 sits in Chapter I and has applied since 2 February 2025, and it is not listed among the fineable provisions in Article 99(4).
frame_summary: The legislature is arguing that a uniform duty to deliver a measured level of workforce AI capability is unworkable across the whole economy, so the duty should be recast as documented effort supported by public authorities rather than a guaranteed outcome.

title: Cedefop updates Skills Forecast: new data to guide Europe's skills and labour market policy to 2035
key_claim: The 2026 Skills Forecast projects EU-27 employment growth of over 4% between 2023 and 2035, with the labour force aged 65 and over growing at over 7% a year and the 30-54 cohort shrinking by 0.2% a year. The Labour Skills and Shortage Index flags mounting pressure in high-skilled occupations, managers, professionals and associate professionals, driven by strong demand, high replacement needs and qualification mismatches.
frame_summary: Cedefop is arguing that Europe's binding skills problem to 2035 is replacement and mismatch in high-skilled occupations rather than aggregate job growth, which makes the composition of training provision, not its volume, the policy variable.

publisher: Aspen Institute (UpSkill America, Economic Opportunities Program)
title: Adult Working Learners Vote With Their Feet: What Employers Are Learning About Foundational Skills
key_claim: Drawing on a mid-August 2026 session and the unreleased 2026 Room for Growth survey, just over half of employers already offer some kind of foundational skills training, more than offer AI training or apprenticeships. Tyson Foods reports 91% annualised retention for on-site Upward Academy participants, and team members paid to attend during shift learned twice as fast on identical content as those attending unpaid. CJK Group cut the path to master operator from six-plus years to two, with 34% of current senior operators coming through the programme in three years. PIAAC places US adults 14th in literacy and 24th in numeracy of 31 nations.
frame_summary: Aspen is arguing that employers already closing foundational skills gaps are doing it quietly and are measuring the payoff in retention and time to competence rather than in wages, which is a different success test from the one wage-return studies apply.

title: As Employers Plan for Growth, Workforce Pressures Continue to Mount (2026 US Workforce Trends Report: Talent Benchmarks)
date_evidence: ### As Employers Plan for Growth, Workforce Pressures Continue to Mount 09/09/2026 ... ROLLING MEADOWS, Ill., Sept. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/
key_claim: Survey of 3,717 US employers collected January to March 2026. 61% anticipate revenue growth by 2027 while only 50% expect headcount to increase. 63% reported annual turnover of 10% or higher in 2025. 73% expect to increase AI adoption in HR by 2028, and employers expect an average of 28 months before AI returns outweigh implementation costs.
frame_summary: Gallagher is arguing that employers are committing to growth they cannot staff, so capability has to be manufactured inside the existing workforce rather than hired in, which puts the quality of internal development on the critical path.

title: In tough job market, microcredentials give grads edge
key_claim: Reporting a Coursera survey of 3,500 students, employers and higher education leaders across seven countries conducted in February and March 2026: 94% of employers say they are inclined to offer higher starting salaries to candidates with microcredentials, 92% say entry-level workers with microcredentials perform better in their first year, and 60% would choose a less experienced candidate holding a generative AI credential over a more experienced one without.
frame_summary: Inside Higher Ed is arguing that microcredentials have become a real hiring and salary differentiator, which makes it the clearest available statement of employer belief about what certification is worth, against which the OECD's measured wage associations can be read.
verbatim_quote: Sixty percent of employers said they would choose a less experienced candidate with a generative AI credential over a more experienced candidate without one, the report said.
verbatim_list: 94 percent of employers say they’re inclined to offer higher starting salaries to candidates with microcredentials
A similar share of employers (92 percent) also report that entry-level workers with microcredentials perform better in their first year.
